terms.definition: Jeevan — a constitutionally complete atom and sentient unit, the seer of the physicochemical world; it is immortal and continuous, while birth and death are occurrences.
Omnipresence — the eternally present, all-pervading reality: formless, motionless absolute energy in which every unit is saturated and through which regulation is manifest.
Time — duration of an activity.
Sanskar — accepted qualitative establishments; in education–sanskar, the establishment and transmission of understanding through human tradition.
Coexistence — sentient and insentient nature saturated in Omnipresence, with mutuality expressed as conflict-free harmony, complementarity, development, and evolution.
Unit — a bounded, countable entity in nature; units may be insentient or sentient.
Existence — infinite sentient and insentient units saturated in Omnipresence: what is, present through development, awakening, and orderliness.
Activity — the inseparable presence of effort, motion, and result; the combined presence of state and motion.
Saturated — immersed, encompassed, and imbued in Omnipresence.
Constitutional completeness — the stage at which an atom completes its constitution and becomes a jeevan-atom.
Knowledge — realised understanding of coexistence, jeevan, humane conduct, and participation in overall orderliness.
Unfolding of knowledge — realisation in coexistence becoming expressible as wisdom and science through awakened jeevan.
Realisation Knowledge — sentient and insentient nature, and its infinite units, saturated in Omnipresence; each unit bears form, properties, essential nature, dharma, and orderliness.
Authenticity — the expression of realisation as evidence; in motion it becomes evidence and resolution.
Madhyasth Darshan — the coexistentialist worldview; darshan is the holistic view obtained through perspective, conception, and realisation.
Four orders of nature — material order, biological order, animal order, and knowledge order.
Relationship — a value-bearing mutuality in which expectations arise from relationality and necessity; fulfilment involves recognition, values, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction.
Effort–Motion–Result — the inseparable triad in activity: effort is the grandeur of an existent state, motion spreads its effect, and result is the grandeur of a different existent state.
Perspective — the process of perceiving, understanding, recognising, and evaluating realities.
Dharma — innateness: that from which a unit cannot be separated; for human beings, happiness. It also names one of the humane evaluative perspectives.
Justice — recognising relationships, fulfilling and evaluating their values, and attaining mutual satisfaction.
Truth — that which is uniformly perceivable, existent, and realisable at all times; it includes absolute, relative, and objective truth in existence.
Resolution — the within-self condition of understanding and mental well-being; comprehensive resolution supports prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence.
Delusion — identifying the body as jeevan and living without understanding; awakening is freedom from delusion.
Mystery — a removable lack of clarity whose elimination depends on awakening of the sentient or intellectual aspect.
Illusion (dependent appearance in Advaita) — neither independently absolute nor sheer non-being; empirically operative, but sublated by knowledge of Brahman.
Empirical level in Advaita — the shared waking order in which embodied knowers, objects, ethics, law, and valid cognition operate.
In Advaita, the absolute level of truth, where Brahman alone is real. In Madhyasth Darshan, paramartha maps to benevolent deployment undertaken for resolution and realisation.
In Advaita, Atman is the innermost Self and ultimate perceiver, identical with Brahman. In Madhyasth Darshan, atma is jeevan’s faculty of realisation and authenticity.
Brahman — in Advaita, the non-dual ultimate reality, identical with Atman and described as existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Mun — the anticipating mind in jeevan; its activities include tasting and selection according to hope, and it guides the body.
Buddhi — intellect; jeevan’s faculty of enlightenment and resolve, inspired by atma.
Chitta — the reflective mind; jeevan’s faculty of contemplation and desire, inspired by buddhi.
Vritti — the decisive mind or disposition; jeevan’s faculty of comparison and thought, inspired by chitta.
Nature — infinite sentient and insentient units across four orders and four realms; formful existence bearing form, properties, essential nature, and dharma.
Knowledge order — the human order, whose distinctive capacity is study, understanding, evaluation, and evidence of awakening.
Realisation — direct, steady experience of existence as coexistence in atma, completing comprehension (bodh) and ending delusion (bhram).
Systematic study — disciplined inquiry through listening (shravan), reflection (manan), and living-in-practice (abhyas) aimed at direct realisation rather than verbal memorisation.
Attentive listening — receiving philosophical definitions and proposals accurately as testable hypotheses rather than dogmas for blind belief.
Rational reflection — examining whether a proposal holds consistently across logic, existential reality, and lived human experience.
Direct perception — clear recognition in chitta of a unit’s real form, properties, innate nature, and dharma without projection or sensory distortion.
Comprehension — settled intellectual conviction in buddhi of reality as known through direct perception (sakshatkar), preceding full realisation in atma.
In cognitive practice (samyama), the disciplined quietening of unexamined imagination so reality can be perceived directly; in bodily living (sanyam), self-regulation for health.
Devoted alignment — orienting thought, evaluation, and action toward human and divine conduct on the basis of understanding rather than ritual appeasement.
Awakening — the transition of jeevan from delusion (bhram) to complete understanding of coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct, evidenced in relationships and living.
Pre-awakening evaluative perspectives — evaluating things and people by sensory pleasantness (priya), bodily convenience (hita), or acquisitive advantage (labh).
Awakened evaluative perspectives — evaluating conduct and reality through relational justice (nyaya), all-round resolution (dharma), and existential truth (satya).
Taste-driven — action and consumption guided by shifting sensory preferences and impulse rather than definite human purpose and value.
Value-grounded — evaluation, production, and conduct anchored in definite human values and participation in orderliness.
The three bounded human aspirations — progeny (putreshana), wealth (vitteshana), and social recognition (lokeshana) — fulfilled through resolution and prosperity rather than accumulation.
Prosperity — the settled recognition and experience of producing and having more physical goods than one’s finite family needs, freeing human effort for relationship and understanding.
Right-use — deploying body, mind, and material wealth for nurturing, protection, and societal order rather than indulgence, hoarding, or domination.
Cyclical — production and resource use in which every transformation returns to and enriches nature’s regenerative cycles without depletion or pollution.
Undivided society — humankind living without sectarian, class, or national division through shared understanding, family-based order, and mutual trust.
Universal human order — self-governing social coordination extending across ten stages from the family to the entire planet across education, justice, production, health, and exchange.
Fearlessness — mutual trust and security in society arising when justice and right-use replace exploitation and conflict.
Regulated intake and bodily conduct — nourishing and exercising the body in accord with physiological order so it serves as a healthy instrument of jeevan.
